# pcg-ts — agent guide

pcg-ts is a deterministic procedural content generation library for
TypeScript (browser + Node, ESM, package `pcg-ts`, optional three.js
adapter `pcg-ts/three`, optional WebGPU field evaluation `pcg-ts/gpu`).
It combines a domain-based attribute data model
(SoA typed arrays), deferred field expressions, a memoizing node-graph
executor, and a hierarchical streaming runtime. It is designed to be
driven programmatically: node capabilities are enumerable at runtime
(`listNodeTypes()`), graphs round-trip through versioned JSON
(`serializeGraph`/`deserializeGraph`), and all errors are actionable.

## Core mental model

- Data flows through graphs as collections of items: geometry items,
  value items (plain numbers/strings/bools), instances items (transform
  batches for renderers). Items carry tags and a revision id (`rev`).
- A `Geometry` holds four attribute domains: point, vertex, primitive,
  detail (always 1 element), plus topology (vertex->point map, primitive
  vertex ranges). Point-only clouds are the common fast path.
- Attributes are named typed-array columns (f32/i32/u32/bool/string)
  with a tuple size. Standard point attributes: P (f32x3), rot (quat
  f32x4, xyzw), scale (f32x3), density (f32), boundsMin/boundsMax
  (f32x3), color (f32x4), seed (u32).
- A `Field` is a deferred computation resolved per element of a domain.
  Field-capable node params accept a constant OR a field expression;
  scalars broadcast against tuples.
- Cooking pulls from declared graph outputs, topologically, memoizing
  each node on (type, param hash, node seed, input item revs).
  `cook(graph, { outputs: ["name"] })` cooks only the named outputs'
  upstream subgraph; untouched nodes keep their caches, so staged
  pipelines (cook output A, bind data, cook output B) fit in one graph.

## Authoring a graph as JSON

Format (`SerializedGraph`, formatVersion 1 — field names exactly):

- `formatVersion`: 1
- `seed`: number (graph seed; node seeds derive from it)
- `nodes`: [{ `id`: string, `type`: registered type name, `params`: object }]
  Omitted params take their schema defaults. Field-capable params accept
  a field spec object (below) instead of a constant. A `subgraph` node
  additionally carries `subgraph: { graph, inputs, outputs, params }` —
  the inner graph recursively in this same format, the exposed pin
  mappings (`{ name, node, pin }` each), and the exposed-param
  declarations (`{ name, targets, description, default, min?, max? }`;
  `type`/`enum`/`acceptsField` are re-derived from the targets on load,
  never read from JSON) — so nested subgraphs round-trip. Its own
  `params` hold the exposed params' values. INSTEAD of `subgraph` it may
  carry `ref: { name, hash? }`, referencing a subgraph registered with
  `registerSubgraph` (below); the two keys are mutually exclusive and no
  other node type may carry either. A
  `dataInput` node serializes with `items: []` (live DataItems are
  runtime-injected; re-bind after deserializing).
- `connections`: [{ `from`: [nodeId, outputPin], `to`: [nodeId, inputPin] }]
- `outputs`: [{ `id`: nodeId, `pin`: outputPin, `name`: result key }]

The key sets above are COMPLETE, at EVERY object position: the graph
object, a node object, a `subgraph` payload, a `ref`, a connection, a
declared output, an exposed-pin declaration, an exposed-param declaration
and each of its `targets`. An unknown key at any of them is a hard error
naming it and listing the valid ones. The format is closed: a future
field arrives with a `formatVersion` bump, not by riding along unnoticed,
and there is no annotation key (descriptive text goes in `meta`, or in an
exposed param's own `description`).

An exposed-param declaration carries ONLY { `name`, `targets`,
`description`, `default`?, `min`?, `max`? }. Writing `type`, `enum` or
`acceptsField` on one is refused by name: the schema is derived from the
targets' registered schemas, so a declaration cannot claim a type or a
field capability the inner params do not have.

Complete minimal example (deserializes and cooks as-is):

```json
{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "seed": 42,
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "scatter", "type": "pointScatterInBounds",
      "params": { "count": 500, "boundsMin": [0, 0, 0], "boundsMax": [50, 0, 50] } },
    { "id": "jitter", "type": "jitterPoints",
      "params": { "amount": { "fn": "fbm", "base": "perlinNoise", "opts": { "frequency": 0.05 } } } }
  ],
  "connections": [ { "from": ["scatter", "out"], "to": ["jitter", "in"] } ],
  "outputs": [ { "id": "jitter", "pin": "out", "name": "points" } ]
}
```

```ts
import { deserializeGraph, serializeGraph, cook, firstGeometry } from "pcg-ts";
const graph = deserializeGraph(json);      // validates everything, names faults
const result = await cook(graph);          // { outputs, stats }
const geo = firstGeometry(result.outputs.points);
serializeGraph(graph);                     // back to JSON (see round-trip note)
```

Round-trip semantics, stated precisely because agents diff JSON: the
output is semantically identical and cooks byte-identically, but it is
NOT textually equal to hand-authored input that omitted params —
serialization writes every param explicitly, filling omitted ones with
their schema defaults. It is idempotent from then on
(`serialize(deserialize(x)) === serialize(deserialize(serialize(deserialize(x))))`).
So compare round-tripped JSON against a round-tripped baseline, never
against your minimal source, and treat newly-appearing default params
as normalization rather than corruption.

## Authoring a graph in code

```ts
import { Graph, cook, pointScatterInBounds, jitterPoints } from "pcg-ts";
const g = new Graph(42);
const a = g.add(pointScatterInBounds, { count: 500 });
const b = g.add(jitterPoints, { amount: [0.5, 0, 0.5] });
g.connect(a, "out", b, "in");
g.output(b, "out", "points");
const { outputs, stats } = await cook(g); // stats: { cooked, cached, elapsedMs }
```

## Graph mutation and introspection (editor/tooling surface)

Every mutation bumps the graph version; the introspection reads are
frozen snapshots with no mutation path that bypasses version bumps.

- `graph.removeNode(handle)` — removes the node, every connection
  touching it, and every output declared on it (documented cascade); one
  version bump; the removed node's cached outputs are dropped
  immediately. Next cook: former downstream nodes recook, untouched
  branches keep serving their caches. Unknown handles (another graph's,
  or already removed) throw. Removing a subgraph *instance* leaves its
  def and inner graph intact.
- `graph.disconnect(from, "pin", to, "pin")` — removes one matching
  connection, returns `true`. Unknown nodes or pins THROW (naming the
  offender, listing valid pins); a missing connection between valid
  endpoints returns `false` with no version bump. On a `multi` input the
  remaining connections keep insertion order (order is part of
  determinism). Cache contract as removeNode: target and downstream
  recook, untouched branches stay cached.
- `graph.removeOutput(name)` — undeclares a terminal output; the name is
  free to redeclare; unknown names throw, listing declared outputs. Node
  caches untouched (outputs change what a cook pulls, not memo keys), so
  the next cook serves every unchanged node from cache.
- `graph.describe()` — frozen structural snapshot: `{ nodes: [{ id,
  seed, defType }], connections: [{ from: [id, pin], to: [id, pin] }],
  outputs: [{ id, pin, name }] }` in insertion/creation/declaration
  order. `seed` is the derived per-node seed the executor uses; `defType`
  is `undefined` when a def carries no usable type string. Cheap enough
  to call per UI frame. Reports structure verbatim — for a
  subgraph-wrapped graph that includes injected plumbing, which
  serialization excludes.
- `graph.getParams(handle)` — frozen shallow copy of the node's current
  params at call time (later setParam calls not reflected). Nested
  values are live references under the library-wide aliasing rule: treat
  them as frozen, change params only through `setParam`.
- `describeSubgraphPins(def)` — per-instance pins of a `subgraphNode`
  def: frozen `{ inputs, outputs }` of `{ name, kind }` in exposure
  order, kinds resolved live from the recorded spec through nested
  subgraphs. Returns `undefined` for non-subgraph defs; throws
  (GraphValidationError, naming pin and inner node) when later edits
  broke the wrapper.
- `describeSubgraphParams(def)` — per-instance params of a `subgraphNode`
  def: frozen list of `{ name, schema, targets }` in exposure order,
  where `schema` is the ParamSchema merged from the inner targets and
  `targets` are the `{ node, param }` slots the value is written into.
  Returns `undefined` for non-subgraph defs; throws when later edits
  removed a bound inner node or param.
- `resolveExposedParam(inner, decl)` — build one exposed param for
  `subgraphNode`'s fourth argument. `decl` is
  `{ name, targets, description, default?, min?, max? }`; the schema is
  DERIVED from the targets' registered schemas (identical `type`/`enum`
  required across targets, `acceptsField` ANDed, bounds intersected) and
  the default is the first target's live value unless overridden. Values
  live on the wrapping instance (so instances tune independently and
  cache independently) and are written into the inner graph at cook time
  and restored afterwards, so cooking never modifies the inner graph and
  a graph's serialized bytes never depend on what was cooked — not even a
  cook of another graph sharing the definition, or one that threw. A
  Field on a param that is not field-capable throws at cook time, naming
  the exposed param and the offending inner target. Two exposed params
  binding the same inner slot, or one listing a slot twice, is a hard
  error naming the params and the slot.
- `registerSubgraph(name, spec)` — publish a subgraph under a name so
  serialized graphs can reference it with `ref: { name, hash? }` instead
  of embedding it. `spec` is `{ graph, inputs?, outputs?, params? }` where
  `graph` is a live `Graph` or a `SerializedGraph` and the rest are the
  serialized exposed-pin / exposed-param declarations. The registry stores
  a canonicalized RECIPE (`serializeGraph(deserializeGraph(...))`), never
  a live graph: `subgraphNode` mutates what it wraps, so every reference
  materializes a fresh graph and def through the same
  `deserializeGraph` → `subgraphNode` path an embedded payload takes.
  Hence: a reference and an embedded copy of one recipe cook
  byte-identically (same bytes, same cache decisions, same memo key,
  within one build); two references to one name share no inner graph and
  no caches; and the registry is not a live-update channel (resolution
  happens once at load; duplicate names throw; there is no unregister).
  Returns `{ name, subgraph, hash, meta? }`, frozen.
- `getRegisteredSubgraph(name)` / `hasRegisteredSubgraph(name)` /
  `listSubgraphs()` — lookup (throws listing every registered name),
  membership, and the full list in registration order.
- `subgraphContentHash(payload)` — 16 hex digits. COVERS node ids, types
  and param values, connections, declared outputs, exposed pin mappings,
  and each exposed param's name/targets/default/bounds; a nested `ref`
  contributes the referenced NAME, not its content. EXCLUDES `meta`,
  graph `seed`s and exposed-param `description`s at every level (none can
  change a cooked byte, and hashing `meta` would make a typo fix break
  every pinned graph). Object keys are sorted, so reordering a param
  schema does not move a hash. Stable within one build only.
- `ref.hash` is OPTIONAL: absent means "the registry's current version"
  and upgrades freely; present means the author pinned it and a mismatch
  is a hard error naming both hashes. Neither mode warns; neither cooks a
  near-miss.
- Subgraph nesting must be acyclic and is enforced statically: `Graph.add`
  refuses a node whose def wraps the graph it is added to (directly or
  through a chain), `registerSubgraph` refuses a recipe referencing the
  name being registered, and `deserializeGraph` refuses a name cycle.
  Editing a referenced primitive's inner graph in place and then
  serializing is refused, rather than silently writing the registry's
  content back out.

Mutations keep serialization consistent: `serializeGraph` of a mutated
graph round-trips and cooks identically. Rebuilding via
`deserializeGraph` instead of mutating discards all warm caches.

## Field-expression JSON grammar

A field spec is `{ "fn": <name>, ...args }`. Entries in `args` arrays
may be nested specs, finite numbers, or number arrays (plain values wrap
into `constant`). All 40 fns (`listFieldFns()`):

- Inputs:
  - `{ fn: "constant", value: 1 | [1, 2, 3] }`
  - `{ fn: "attribute", name: "density", tupleSize?: 1 }` (numeric attrs only)
  - `{ fn: "position" }` — reads P (tuple 3); `{ fn: "index" }` — 0,1,2,...
  - `{ fn: "randomField", key?: 0 | "salt" }` — per-element hash random in [0,1)
- Elementwise, `args` with exact arity (scalars broadcast; f64 math, f32 storage):
  - 2 args: `add sub mul div min max lt le gt ge eq dot atan2`
    (comparisons emit 1/0; `dot` reduces tuples to a scalar; `atan2`
    args are [y, x], radians)
  - 1 arg: `abs floor length normalize sin cos tan asin acos atan`
    (trig in radians, elementwise)
  - 3 args: `clamp` (x, lo, hi), `lerp` (a, b, t), `select` (cond, a, b)
  - 5 args: `remap` (x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax; unclamped)
- Structure:
  - `{ fn: "vec", args: [x, y, z] }` — 1+ args, concatenates components
  - `{ fn: "component", args: [tupleField], index: 0 }` — extract one component
  - `{ fn: "ramp", args: [scalarField], stops: [[0, 0], [1, 1]] }` —
    piecewise-linear through [position, value] stops, strictly ascending,
    clamped at the ends
- Noise (scalar fields of the sample position; pure function of seed +
  position — the context seed does not affect them):
  - `{ fn: "valueNoise" | "perlinNoise" | "simplexNoise", opts?: {
      seed?: int, frequency?: number, offset?: [x, y, z], position?: spec,
      normalized?: false } }`
    valueNoise in [0,1); perlin/simplex approx [-1,1]
  - `{ fn: "worleyNoise", opts?: { ...same, output?: "f1" | "f2" | "f2-f1",
      exact?: false } }`
    (distance to nearest/2nd-nearest feature point; f1 in [0, ~1.73);
    `exact: true` widens the cell search until provably exhaustive —
    slower, use when the fast approximation's rare artifacts matter)
  - `{ fn: "fbm", base: "perlinNoise" | "valueNoise" | "simplexNoise" | "worleyNoise",
      opts?: { ...same, octaves?: 4, lacunarity?: 2, gain?: 0.5 } }`
    (sum not renormalized: range grows toward base * (1-gain^octaves)/(1-gain))
  - `normalized: true` (any noise, fbm included) affinely remaps the
    documented raw range to exactly [0, 1]. Raw ranges are
    machine-readable: `NOISE_RAW_RANGES` (per noise type) and
    `noiseOutputRange(field)` (per field instance, fbm-aware).

Nested example — density in [0,1] from remapped 4-octave noise:

```json
{ "fn": "clamp", "args": [
    { "fn": "remap", "args": [
        { "fn": "fbm", "base": "perlinNoise", "opts": { "frequency": 0.03, "octaves": 4 } },
        -1, 1, 0, 1 ] },
    0, 1 ] }
```

In code, both `fieldFromJson(spec)` fields and combinator-composed
fields serialize back via `fieldToJson` — a combinator derives its spec
from its arguments, so since v0.9 a graph holding
`mul(position(), 0.1)` serializes (before v0.9 `serializeGraph` threw
and pointed at `fieldFromJson`). Four cases refuse: a `makeField`
closure; any field composed over one (the absent spec propagates); a
tree deeper than 256 levels — derivation refuses at exactly the depth
`fieldFromJson` parses, so a spec that could not be re-parsed is never
produced and no graph is written that cannot be read back; and an
argument the constructor accepts but the grammar's parser rejects (a
fractional `seed`, a non-finite `frequency`/`offset`/`constant`/`ramp`
stop, an fbm `base` outside the built-in factories, `-0` anywhere).
`fieldToJson` names the ONE cause that applied and the fix for it — for
an opaque leaf it names that leaf's structural key, so a `makeField`
buried deep in a combinator tree is identified rather than the
constructor that noticed it; for an ungrammatical argument the message
leads with the offending option (e.g. `` `seed` must be an integer ``).
`serializeGraph` prefixes any of them with `node "<id>" param "<key>": `.
Note this is about DESCRIBING a field, not about where it runs: device
eligibility is narrower and additionally requires either an AUTHORED
spec or `acceptDerivedSpecs` (see the GPU section).

## Node types (full schemas: docs/nodes.md, machine-readable: docs/nodes.json)

`listNodeTypes()` entries carry an optional `category` grouping label
(absent when a type declared none); the standard library is fully
categorized: source, sampler, point op, filter, attribute, value,
spawn, io, composite.

- attributeReduce — reduce an attribute across a domain to one detail value (sum/min/max/average/count); unlike promoteAttribute it writes under its own `outName` (so a min and a max can coexist), adds `count`, and SKIPS non-finite values instead of propagating them
- attributeRemap — remap an attribute's range: `range` maps a stated [inMin, inMax] onto [outMin, outMax], `fit` measures the actual finite range first (the only way to normalize, since no param can read a value out of the geometry); NaN stays NaN rather than becoming a valid-looking number
- copyToPoints — copy a source cloud onto every target point, composing transforms and seeds
- dataInput — emit externally injected DataItems (`items` set via graph.setParam; serializes as `items: []`, re-bind live data after deserializing)
- filterByAttribute — keep points where a scalar/string attribute passes a comparison
- filterByBounds — keep points inside/outside an axis-aligned box
- filterByDensity — keep points by `density` (threshold or probabilistic)
- filterByExpression — keep points where a field-capable boolean `predicate` is positive; NaN never survives (`v>0||v<0`, not `!==0`), and a tuple>1 predicate is refused rather than broadcast
- jitterPoints — deterministic random offset per point (field-capable amount)
- mergePoints — concatenate point clouds (multi input), union of attributes
- meshPrimitive — SOURCE of triangle-mesh geometry in-graph: a subdivided `plane` (orientation xz/xy/yz, normal along the positive third axis) or a `box` (six faces, per-face points so uv seams are exact); emits P, uv and `poly` primitives. This is the only way to make mesh geometry from JSON — dataInput carries nothing through serialization — so it is what feeds surfaceSample, transferAttribute raycast/uv, and splineSample's mesh-side neighbours
- orientAlongVector — write `rot` quaternions so a local axis (default `+z`) follows a field-capable direction (e.g. a tangent/normal attribute), `up` hint fixes roll; zero directions keep their rot
- partitionByAttribute — split into per-value point clouds, tagged `name=value`
- pointGrid — regular grid of points
- pointLine — evenly spaced points on a segment
- pointNeighborhood — per-point neighbour statistics from the shared uniform grid: a count within `radius`, and optionally the average of another attribute over those neighbours; `maxCount` keeps the NEAREST N (ties to lower index) and accumulation is always in ascending point index, so a capped average is bit-stable; a point with no neighbours averages to its OWN value, so differences like `P - nbrP` are exactly zero for isolates
- pointScatterInBounds — uniform random points in a box
- projectToPlane — orthogonal projection of points onto a plane
- promoteAttribute — move an attribute between domains (first/average/sum/min/max)
- removeAttribute — delete named attributes from a domain (`strict` errors on a missing name); refuses to delete point `P`
- sampleNearestPoint — look up the nearest point of a second `source` cloud per point: distance, source index, and optionally copy one of its attributes; misses report distance Infinity / index -1 and leave a copied attribute at its prior value
- selfPrune — greedy minimum-distance thinning (lowest index wins)
- setAttribute — create/overwrite an attribute from a field-capable value; `type: "string"` picks per element from a `values` list by numeric selector (floor+clamp, total) or writes a constant `stringValue`; optional `seed` param folds into the field evaluation (0 = node seed unchanged)
- setBounds — stamp boundsMin/boundsMax on every point
- spawnInstances — terminal: points to render-agnostic instance batches (4x4 column-major transforms); `assetAttr` names a string attribute for per-point asset ids (empty entries fall back to `assetId`); one batch per asset in ascending first-occurrence point order, instances within a batch in ascending point order
- splineSample — arc-length sampling along polyline primitives (emits tangent, curveU)
- subgraph — composite node wrapping an inner graph; create with `subgraphNode(inner, inputs, outputs, params)` (pins AND params are per-instance), inspect with `getSubgraphSpec` / `describeSubgraphPins` / `describeSubgraphParams`, serializes recursively as `subgraph` or by name as `ref`
- surfaceSample — area-weighted scatter on a triangle mesh with density acceptance (emits normal)
- transferAttribute — transfer an attribute from a `source` geometry onto the input's points; `mapping`: "nearest" (closest source point in 3D, never misses), "uv" (destination point-domain UVs located in the source triangulation's UV space; source UVs read from the vertex domain when present — seam-correct — else point), "raycast" (forward-only ray per point: `direction` or per-point `directionAttr`, nearest hit, optional `maxDistance`). uv/raycast need a triangle source; f32 interpolates barycentrically, i32/u32/bool/string take the dominant corner (largest weight, ties → first corner); shared-edge/equal-distance ties → lowest source primitive index; misses keep the prior value (attribute default if new), count reportable via `missCountAttr` (u32 detail); `attrDomain: "vertex"` reads per-corner source values. Grid acceleration is result-neutral; epsilon policy exported (TRANSFER_BARY_EPS, TRANSFER_AREA_EPS, TRANSFER_DET_EPS, TRANSFER_BOX_PAD_REL)
- transformPoints — per-point translate/rotate/scale, composing with rot/scale attrs (field-capable)
- valueConstant — emit a constant number as a value item
- volumeSample — jittered grid fill of a box or of the input geometry's bounds

## Key invariants and contracts

- Determinism: all randomness derives from seeds via PCG32 + 32-bit hash
  combining. Same graph + seed = byte-identical output across runs,
  platforms, cook orders, and streaming paths. Seed chain: graph seed ->
  node seed = hashCombine(graphSeed, hashString(nodeId)) -> per-point
  hashCombine(seed, index, axis). No Math.random anywhere.
- Purity: node execute treats inputs as immutable and uses only its
  derived seed. The executor memoizes on exactly (type, params, seed,
  input revs); params hash structurally (Fields by their stable key,
  DataItems by rev — geometry is never deep-hashed).
- Cook results are immutable: `CookResult` collections alias live cache
  internals. Clone with `cloneGeometry(geo)` before mutating. Arrays
  bound into params (e.g. dataInput `items`) are captured by reference —
  treat as frozen after binding; bind a fresh array to change data.
- Column lifetime: an evaluated field Column may alias attribute storage
  and is valid only until the geometry is mutated or resized; results
  memoize per EvalContext object, so make a fresh context after mutation.
- Cache invalidation is automatic via memo keys (param edits, seed
  changes, input rev changes, subgraph inner-graph edits). Cancelling a
  cook (AbortSignal -> CookCancelledError) keeps finished nodes' caches.

## World streaming (hierarchical runtime)

`new World({ seed, levels, maxCellsPerLevel?, onCellReady?, onCellEvicted? })`
streams grid cells per level around a viewpoint. Levels are ordered
coarse to fine (optionally one leading unbounded level); each is a
`LevelDef`:

- `name`, `graph`, `bind(graph, ctx)` — required.
- `cellSize`: number (cell edge, world units) or `"unbounded"` (one
  global cell, must be the first level).
- `cellMode?`: `"xz"` (default — square XZ cells, unbounded in Y,
  coords `[cx, cz]`) or `"xyz"` (cube cells, coords `[cx, cy, cz]`,
  radii in full XYZ distance). Nesting: like under like; `"xyz"` under
  `"xz"` uses the containing XZ column as parent; `"xz"` under a
  bounded `"xyz"` parent is rejected at construction; an unbounded
  parent accepts either mode.
- `generationRadius?`: cells cook when their center enters this radius.
  Required (positive) for bounded levels; omit for an unbounded level
  (a value is accepted and ignored there).
- `retainRadius?`: eviction hysteresis, default generationRadius * 1.25.
- `cookOutputs?`: cook only these declared outputs of the graph per
  cell (per-output cooking; names validated at construction). Omit to
  cook all.

Before each cell cook, `bind(graph, ctx)` wires the `CellContext` into
the graph — the only channel for cell data. `ctx` is a discriminated
union on `cellMode`: `{ cellMode, coord, min, max, levelIndex,
levelName, seed, parent? }` with 2D coord/min/max for `"xz"` (and
unbounded) levels, 3D for `"xyz"`. Contract: derive params only from
ctx, and wire `ctx.seed` (= hashCombine(worldSeed, levelIndex,
...coord) — every cell coordinate is hashed) into every stochastic
node. Sanctioned seeding: set seed params per node (vary with
hashCombine(ctx.seed, n); setAttribute's `seed` param folds in as
hashCombine(nodeSeed, seed), 0 = unchanged), or reseed the whole graph
via `graph.setSeed(...)` inside bind — memo keys include seeds and
bind-time writes never count as user edits, so neither causes phantom
recooks. Parent-cell outputs arrive as `ctx.parent.outputs`; inject
them via a dataInput node. `await world.update([x, y, z], { budgetMs?,
signal?, maxCooksPerUpdate? })` cooks nearest-first, evicts by
retainRadius + LRU, and reports { cooked, evicted, pending }.
`world.invalidate(level?, coord?)` forces recooks; parent recooks
cascade staleness to children automatically.

## GPU field evaluation (pcg-ts/gpu)

The serializable field-expression grammar (previous section) is the GPU
surface: every fn compiles to WGSL.

DESCRIBING vs RUNNING — two questions since v0.9, do not conflate them:
- `getFieldSpec(field)` answers "can this field be described": a spec
  for both `fieldFromJson` fields (AUTHORED) and combinator fields
  (DERIVED), `undefined` only for a `makeField` closure, anything
  composed over one, or a tree past 256 levels.
- Device eligibility is NARROWER: an authored spec always, a derived
  spec only when the resolver advertises `acceptDerivedSpecs: true`
  (default false). With it off a derived-spec field evaluates on the
  CPU and counts a `"derived-spec"` fallback — NOT `"no-spec"`, which
  now means genuinely undescribable.
- Opt-in on purpose: derived and authored forms of one expression
  compile to the same kernel key and the same WGSL and produce the same
  bytes (measured, one adapter), but the GPU path is still a documented
  approximation of the CPU reference. Turning the gate on by default
  would move output bytes for graphs that already pass a resolver and
  never asked, including discrete flips at knife-edge compares. The
  memo salt protects cache correctness, not output stability, so
  adoption is the caller's explicit choice per evaluator.

One eligible field = one compute dispatch over the whole domain
(chunked into several `dispatchWorkgroups` calls past 65535 × 64 ≈
4.19M elements, byte-invisibly). Chains of fusable nodes go further:
they cook as one device-resident run with a single readback (see
"Device-resident runs" below).

Setup (browser):

```ts
import { cook } from "pcg-ts";
import { GpuFieldEvaluator } from "pcg-ts/gpu";
const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const device = await adapter.requestDevice();
const gpu = new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { adapterInfo: adapter.info });
const result = await cook(graph, { gpu });   // CookOptions.gpu
```

Node: `npm i -D webgpu` (Dawn bindings; the library has no dependency
on it), then `const adapter = await create([]).requestAdapter()` with
`import { create } from "webgpu"`.

Surface:

- `GpuFieldResolver` (core interface, no WebGPU types): `{ cacheSalt:
  string; residentTerminals?: readonly string[]; acceptDerivedSpecs?:
  boolean; resolveField(field, ctx, stats?): Promise<Column> | null;
  planRun?; executeRun? }` — `acceptDerivedSpecs` is the SINGLE source
  of truth for derived-spec eligibility: the executor reads it to
  decide both the memo-key salt and fusion, and the resolver must act
  on exactly the same value, or it produces GPU bytes under a CPU memo
  key. The two run methods are optional and
  detailed under "Device-resident runs" below; absence degrades to
  per-node cooking with identical bytes.
  `null` is returned synchronously for ineligible fields — the caller
  falls back to the CPU `evaluateField` and the reason is counted. A
  non-null return commits to GPU: it resolves to a freshly allocated
  column (never a view of attribute storage) with the same element type
  and tuple size the CPU would produce; a rejection is an error (device
  failure), never a silent fallback.
- `CookOptions.gpu?: GpuFieldResolver` / `WorldOptions.gpu?` /
  `UpdateOptions.gpu?` (update wins, threaded to every cell cook) /
  `captureAsync(geo, domain, field, seed?, gpu?, stats?)` — the
  graph-free entry point; without `gpu` it is byte-identical to
  `capture`.
- `CookStats.gpu` (present exactly when the cook was given a resolver;
  includes nested subgraph-cook work): `{ dispatches,
  pipelinesCompiled, pipelineCacheHits, residentRuns, fusedNodes,
  readbacksSaved, fallbacks: Record<reason, count> }`.
  `dispatches` = **kernels**, one per resolved field column plus one
  apply kernel per fused member — NOT `dispatchWorkgroups` calls; a
  chunked kernel still counts once (a 4.3M-point 4-member run reports
  4 while issuing 8). Exactly one kernel counts more than once: a
  MULTI-ASSET spawner terminal dispatches once per asset present in the
  input, over that asset's element range and into that asset's output
  buffer, so the unit is (step, asset), not step. Those are distinct
  dispatches over disjoint ranges, not chunks of one range. A
  constant-`assetId` spawn has exactly one asset and still counts 1, so
  v0.7 numbers stay comparable. The complete fallback-reason
  vocabulary:
  - `no-spec` — the field cannot be described at all: a `makeField`
    closure, anything composed over one, a tree past 256 levels, or an
    argument the grammar's parser rejects
  - `derived-spec` — the field describes itself, but its spec was
    DERIVED by the combinator API and this resolver does not advertise
    `acceptDerivedSpecs`. Scoped to the PER-FIELD seam only: a node the
    same setting keeps out of a fused run is not counted again at the
    fusion gate, since its fields still fall back per-field and one
    cause reported twice would read as two
  - `compile-error` — spec cannot lower to WGSL against the geometry's
    attribute layout (missing or string attribute, tuple size > 4,
    non-finite f32 constant)
  - `too-many-buffers` — kernel needs > 8 storage buffers (more than 7
    attribute inputs + the output; baseline WebGPU limit)
  - `run-plan-failed` — some member of a resident run cannot be
    compiled into the pipeline (unknown resident kind, field compile
    error, tuple/layout mismatch, missing standard attribute, buffer
    limit). Counted once per rejected run; every member then cooks
    per-node, including surfacing the identical CPU error for genuinely
    invalid params.
  - `run-too-large` — a run's resident working set exceeds
    `maxResidentBytes`. Counted once per rejected run.
  - NODE-level opt-outs (`ResidentDesc.eligible` returning a reason
    string) are part of this vocabulary in principle, but the standard
    node library declares NONE. Every reason a standard node stays off
    the device today is one of the per-field or per-run reasons above.
    v0.7's `spawn-asset-attr` was the only one and v0.8 retired it:
    `spawnInstances` is device-resident with `assetAttr` set as well.
  - Element count is NEVER a fallback reason; `dispatch-too-large` no
    longer exists (chunking removed it).
- `NodeDef.gpu?: "fields" | "always"` — GPU-adoption marker. `"fields"`
  on `setAttribute`, `transformPoints`, `jitterPoints`,
  `orientAlongVector`, `surfaceSample`, `volumeSample`; `"always"` on
  subgraph defs (they forward the resolver to inner cooks and their
  counters land in the outermost sink). When a cook has a resolver and
  such a node has a live Field param this resolver WOULD accept
  (authored, or derived with the gate on), the memo key gains
  `|gpu:<cacheSalt>` — so toggling gpu never serves bytes produced by
  the other path, while nodes with no acceptable field param keep their
  cache hits across the toggle. The marker is conservative: it applies
  for eligible-but-uncompilable fields too (over-invalidation; bytes
  stay CPU-identical). `GpuFieldEvaluator`'s salt is
  `"gpu2|<vendor>|<architecture>|<device>|<description>"` (format
  version + adapter identity; missing fields become `?`) — bytes from
  different devices never serve each other. The executor appends
  `+derived` to that salt when `acceptDerivedSpecs` is on and appends
  NOTHING when it is off, so two evaluators on one adapter that
  disagree about the gate cannot collide in the memo cache, and every
  pre-v0.9 key is byte-identical.
- `GpuFieldEvaluatorOptions`: `adapterInfo?` (salt identity when the
  device exposes none); `maxResidentBytes?` (default 512 MiB — the
  resident-run working-set bound); `maxPooledBytes?` (default 256 MiB —
  idle bytes the buffer pool retains; `0` disables retention);
  `maxElementsPerDispatch?` (chunk size override, byte-invisible,
  intended for tests forcing chunk seams — production code leaves it
  unset; default `65535 × workgroupSize` = 4 194 240 at wg 64);
  `deviceInstances?` (default false — opt in to device-resident
  instance transforms; see "Device-resident instancing" below);
  `acceptDerivedSpecs?` (default false — opt in to resolving fields
  whose spec was DERIVED by the combinator API; see "DESCRIBING vs
  RUNNING" above). Both are advertised on the resolver
  (`evaluator.residentTerminals`, `evaluator.acceptDerivedSpecs`) so
  the executor and the resolver decide from one value.
- `evaluator.dispose()` destroys pooled (idle) buffers only; in-flight
  buffers stay valid and re-pool on release and the evaluator remains
  usable (pipeline/kernel caches untouched). DETACHED buffers (device
  transform handles) are untouched too — the pool does not own them.
  `evaluator.poolStats` → `{ buffersCreated, buffersReused,
  buffersDestroyed, pooledBuffers, pooledBytes, buffersDetached,
  detachedBuffers, detachedBytes }`.
- Pipelines cache on the evaluator instance (keyed by kernel
  specialization key = codegen version + spec key + attribute layout)
  and persist across cooks; `pipelineCacheSize` getter for tools.
- `compileFieldSpec(spec, { attributes })` and `supportedGpuFieldFns()`
  are exported for direct WGSL inspection; compile errors are
  actionable (they name the spec node and list what is supported).
- World note: toggling gpu between updates does NOT recook stored
  cells (cell staleness is version-based); provenance protects the
  graph memo layer whenever a cell actually recooks.

Device-resident runs (fusion):

- Opt-in through two OPTIONAL resolver methods, both or neither — the
  executor fuses only when it finds both, so a v0.5-style resolver
  gets exactly the per-node behavior and identical bytes:
  - `planRun?(members: readonly ResidentMemberDesc[], ctx:
    ResidentRunContext, stats?): object | null` — synchronous and
    device-free. `null` = cannot fuse; the resolver counts the reason
    and every member cooks per-node. The returned plan is opaque to the
    executor.
  - `executeRun?(plan: object, input: ResidentRunInput, stats?):
    Promise<ResidentRunResult>` — commits to device execution; a
    rejection is an error, never a silent fallback (except the standard
    cancellation error when `input.signal` aborted). Its `geo` must be
    structurally indistinguishable from cooking the members
    sequentially: same attribute set, shapes, defaults, insertion
    order, string tables, topology; untouched attributes pass through
    byte-identically.
  - `ResidentMemberDesc` = `{ id, type, kind, params, seed }` (`kind`
    from the node def's `resident` descriptor, `seed` exactly what the
    CPU execute would receive). `ResidentRunContext` = `{ attributes:
    Record<name, { type, tupleSize }>, count }`.
- Fusable CHAIN kinds (exactly four, all count-preserving, one geometry
  in / one geometry out): `setAttribute` (numeric mode only — not
  `type: "string"`, `domain: "point"`, empty `values`, empty
  `stringValue`), `transformPoints`, `jitterPoints`,
  `orientAlongVector`. Plus one TERMINAL kind, `spawnInstances`
  (`ResidentDesc.terminal: true`): it may be a run's LAST member, a
  chain never continues through it, and it joins a run only when the
  resolver lists its kind in `residentTerminals` — see
  "Device-resident instancing" below. Additionally, for EVERY member:
  every `Field` in its param tree must carry a spec this resolver
  accepts (authored always; derived only under `acceptDerivedSpecs`),
  so the gate widens which chains fuse as well as which fields resolve.
- Boundary rules — the executor takes MAXIMAL linear chains and stops
  when: the tail has ≠ 1 outgoing connection (any fan-out, counting
  connections to nodes outside this cook's selection), the tail carries
  a declared graph output, the consumer is outside the cooked
  selection, the consumer is not fusable, or the consumer's incoming
  set is not exactly the tail. A chain of length 1 is not a run —
  EXCEPT a lone TERMINAL, which is (see "Device-resident instancing").
  Detection is conservative: it under-fuses, never over-fuses. An
  interior node with external consumers becomes a run terminal with its
  own readback — fusion never changes which bytes the graph observes.
- Cache contract: ONLY the run terminal caches, under
  `run1|gpu:<cacheSalt>|i<first member inputSig>|m[type|s<seed>|p<paramHash>|x<memoKey>]…`
  (one `m[...]` tuple per member, in order). Interior members hold NO
  entry while fused (any stale per-node entry is cleared). Editing any
  member recooks exactly that run; siblings and upstream stay cached.
  Run keys and per-node keys (`<type>|s…`) can never collide, so
  neither path serves the other's bytes — but a node holds ONE memo
  slot, so flipping gpu on/off (or fusion on/off) recooks the chain
  every time BY DESIGN. Benchmark from cold caches.
- Memory: working set = Σ resident slot bytes over every epoch + Σ
  field-temporary column bytes (held for the WHOLE run, not just their
  member) + readback staging bytes, checked against `maxResidentBytes`
  at plan time. Logical bytes only: pow2 pool bucketing can allocate up
  to 2×, and the 12-byte per-chunk uniforms are not counted.
- Cost model: a CONSTANT param (plain number or number tuple) costs a
  16-byte uniform slot and NO dispatch — only field-valued params
  materialize an `n`-element column. Since v0.6.1 the
  `examples/08-gpu-fields` chain holds 120 bytes per point (was 212)
  and issues 9 member kernels (was 12). Constant values live in the
  uniform, never in generated WGSL: the apply-kernel key encodes only
  which params are constant, their tuple sizes, and their slots, so
  editing a constant hits the pipeline cache instead of recompiling.
  A kernel carries at most `MAX_APPLY_CONST_SLOTS` (4) constant slots.
- Third-party `resident` kinds: `NodeDef.resident?: { kind: string;
  eligible?(params): boolean | string; terminal?: boolean }`.
  `eligible` runs outside the executor's error wrapping — it must be
  cheap, pure, and total; an exception there escapes `cook()`
  unwrapped. Returning a non-empty STRING means the same as `false`
  (does not fuse) but names the reason, which the executor counts once
  per cook in `fallbacks` under exactly that key — use it for
  author-actionable cases, plain `false` otherwise. `terminal: true`
  permits output pins beyond the single geometry one (the resolver must
  then model every extra pin) and requires the resolver to advertise
  the kind in `residentTerminals`.

Device-resident instancing (pcg-ts/gpu + pcg-ts/three) — v0.7.0,
multi-asset since v0.8.0:

- Opt in: `new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { deviceInstances: true })`.
  That sets `evaluator.residentTerminals = ["spawnInstances"]`; default
  `[]`, and with `[]` the spawner cooks byte-for-byte as it always has.
- Terminal contract. ANY `spawnInstances` may end a run — constant
  `assetId` and non-empty `assetAttr` alike (v0.7 restricted this to
  `assetAttr === ""`; v0.8 does not). The node declares NO `eligible`
  gate. The run appends a compose-TRS kernel writing one column-major
  4x4 f32 per point (`count * 64` bytes, exactly the `InstanceBatch`
  layout) into ONE BUFFER PER ASSET, each of which it then
  `BufferPool.detach`es. A LONE spawner IS a run under the opt-in (the
  single-node exception: fusion is the only way to produce device
  output at all). When `ResidentRunContext.needsGeometry` is false —
  the terminal's geometry pin is neither connected nor a declared
  output — the run does NO readback: no `mapAsync`, no staging buffer,
  no CPU copy of P/rot/scale. `stats.readbacksSaved` then contributes
  `members`, the one case where
  `readbacksSaved === fusedNodes - residentRuns` fails.
- What the caller receives: the terminal's instances pin carries an
  `InstancesItem` with `deviceBatches?: readonly DeviceInstanceBatch[]`
  (`{ residency: "device", assetId, count, transforms }`), ONE ENTRY
  PER ASSET in the batch order specified below, NOT
  `batches`. Reading `.batches` on it THROWS (naming both fixes) —
  probe with `isDeviceResidentInstances(item)` or
  `item.deviceBatches !== undefined` FIRST. `transforms` is a
  `DeviceTransformsHandle`: `{ backend: string; byteLength: number;
  disposed: boolean; resource: unknown; dispose(): void }` — opaque,
  never a `Float32Array`. `deviceTransformsBuffer(handle)`
  (`pcg-ts/gpu`) narrows `resource` to the backend buffer; bind exactly
  `byteLength` bytes from offset 0 (pool buckets to pow2 — the tail is
  uninitialized). Wrong backend or a disposed handle throws.
- SHARED DEVICE IS MANDATORY. One `GPUDevice` must back both the
  `GpuFieldEvaluator` and the `THREE.WebGPURenderer`: a `GPUBuffer`
  belongs to the device that created it, two devices cannot share one,
  and a WebGL context cannot read a WebGPU buffer at all. Construct as
  `device = await gpuAdapter.requestDevice()` →
  `renderer = new WebGPURenderer({ device })` → `await renderer.init()`
  → `new GpuFieldEvaluator(device, { deviceInstances: true })` →
  `await createWebGpuInstanceAdapter({ renderer, assets })`. A batch
  whose handle's backend is not `"webgpu"` is refused by `build()`.
- Renderer wiring (`pcg-ts/three`): `createWebGpuInstanceAdapter({
  renderer, assets }): Promise<WebGpuInstanceAdapter>` (async — it
  imports `three/webgpu` lazily, so a WebGL app pays nothing), then
  `new WorldThreeBinding({ group, assets, deviceInstances: { adapter,
  bounds? } })`. `bounds(levelName, coord, assetId) => { center, radius
  } | undefined` supplies the sphere out of band, because
  `InstancedMesh.computeBoundingSphere()` would read the (empty) CPU
  matrix array and cull the cell away; `undefined` (or an infinite
  centre, i.e. an unbounded level) disables frustum culling for that
  batch's object instead of guessing, and a non-finite/negative radius
  throws. Called ONCE PER BATCH, not once per cell (v0.8): with one
  sphere per cell every asset inherits the padding of the tallest one,
  so `assetId` is the lever for padding by that asset's own radius.
  Ignoring the third argument keeps the per-cell behaviour and existing
  two-parameter callbacks still type-check.
  Without a `deviceInstances` binding, a device-resident item is an
  ERROR naming both fixes — never a silently empty cell.
  `adapter.stats` → `{ built, released, adopted, liveInstances }`.
- Ownership chain, exactly: pool-owned → `detach` (the run's LAST line,
  after the final cancellation check, so every earlier failure path
  reclaims it) → holder-owned handle → `dispose()`. ONE detach and ONE
  handle PER ASSET, so a multi-asset cell hands out N handles; a
  transfer that fails partway disposes each buffer exactly once.
  Nothing else ever frees them: not the pool, not the memo cache, not
  `GpuFieldEvaluator.dispose()`, not `BufferPool.dispose()`.
  - The GRAPH delivers but never owns: a terminal producing device
    batches writes a `volatile` cache entry (delivered once, then
    refused by the hit path), so device-resident output is NEVER
    memoized and every cook mints a fresh handle. Memoizing would pin
    device memory for the graph's lifetime and hand one handle to two
    owners. A handle no delivered collection carries — or one from a
    failed/cancelled cook — is disposed by the cook, not stranded.
  - `WorldThreeBinding` is the owner of last resort: it refcounts
    handles BY IDENTITY and disposes at the last release only. Identity
    is load-bearing — a child cell forwarding its parent's outputs
    holds the SAME handle object, so parent/child eviction is safe in
    either order. Four release paths: evict, recook (new handles
    retained before old released, so a shared handle survives the
    swap), partial build failure (handles retained for the WHOLE cell
    up front, released in the catch), and `binding.dispose()`.
  - The ADAPTER never disposes a handle; it owns only the
    `InstancedMesh` and its attribute. `adapter.release(object)` frees
    those without destroying the adopted buffer.
  - `dispose()` twice is a no-op, never a double free. Reading
    `resource` after dispose throws.
  - Leaks are VISIBLE: an un-disposed handle stays counted in
    `evaluator.poolStats.detachedBuffers` / `.detachedBytes`; the
    binding reports the same population as `binding.deviceHandleCount`
    / `.deviceHandleBytes` — since v0.8 one handle per BATCH (per asset
    in a cell), not one per cell; both count DISTINCT handles, so a
    handle shared across cells counts once. Steady state over a
    fly-through, not climb.
    Cross-check the COUNTS only: pool bytes are pow2 bucket sizes,
    binding bytes are the logical `count * 64` payload, so the two byte
    totals differ permanently and by design.
  - `deviceHandleBytes` is a LEAK METER, NOT VRAM. It is a lower bound
    on device occupancy and since v0.8 a loose one: the pool buckets to
    the next power of two with a 256-BYTE FLOOR (start at 256, double
    until >= the requested size; internal, no exported symbol), and a
    multi-asset spawn takes one buffer per asset, so a cell with four
    small batches pays four roundings instead of one — a 3-instance
    batch is 192 logical bytes in a 256-byte bucket, a 20-instance
    batch 1280 in 2048. Exact property: retained bytes return to zero
    and stay bounded. `evaluator.poolStats` = `{ buffersCreated,
    buffersReused, buffersDestroyed, pooledBuffers, pooledBytes,
    buffersDetached, detachedBuffers, detachedBytes }`; its byte fields
    are BUCKET bytes.
- MULTI-ASSET GROUPING — part of the device contract, safe to depend
  on. `assetAttr` is device-resident since v0.8. There is NO
  device-side sort: no resident node can produce a string attribute
  (`setAttribute`'s resident predicate requires `type !== "string"`),
  so the asset key is a host column BY CONSTRUCTION. The host plans the
  grouping with the SAME function the CPU spawner (`buildInstanceBatches`)
  calls, uploads a permutation, and the device composes once per asset
  — no atomics, no prefix sum, no readback. Ordering is therefore
  identical on both paths by construction, not by comparison:
  - Batch order = ASCENDING FIRST-OCCURRENCE POINT INDEX of each
    distinct RESOLVED asset id. Not string-table order, not intern
    order, not lexicographic — a recook whose string table interned in
    a different order still produces the same batch order. Points
    `["b","a","b"]` → batches `["b","a"]`, counts `[2,1]`.
  - Within a batch: ASCENDING ORIGINAL POINT INDEX (stable partition).
  - Key resolution per point i: read component 0 of the string
    attribute (only component 0, whatever the tuple size); `""`
    resolves to `assetId` and MERGES into that batch rather than
    opening its own — including when another point carries the literal
    string equal to `assetId`; the merged batch sits at the first
    occurrence of EITHER. An out-of-range string-table index resolves
    to `""` and merges the same way. The table-index → asset-id map is
    NOT injective; never key a batch on a raw table index.
  - Zero points → ZERO batches, in constant mode as well as attribute
    mode. An asset present in the string table but on no point produces
    NO batch: groups come from points, never from the table.
  - `assetAttr` naming a missing attribute, or a non-string attribute,
    is still an ERROR with the CPU spawner's exact message. Both name
    the attribute; the MISSING-attribute form additionally lists the
    string point attributes present, the non-string form names the type
    it got instead. The run planner mirrors those two conditions and
    REJECTS (counting `run-plan-failed`) rather than throwing, so the
    per-node path serves and raises it — exactly one copy of each
    message exists.
- REMAINING BOUNDARY — a string `setAttribute` breaks the fusable
  chain. `setAttribute` is fusable in NUMERIC point-domain mode only,
  so the idiomatic way to COMPUTE an asset key (`type: "string"` with a
  `values` list and a field-capable selector) is not resident and the
  chain breaks THERE. When it feeds the spawner directly (the recipe
  above, and `examples/02-forest`) the run holds ONLY the spawner —
  report fusion depth honestly: one member, not four. Resident nodes
  BETWEEN the string write and the spawn still fuse with it, so depth
  is whatever survives downstream of the break; the chain in FRONT of
  the break fuses as its own run. Recorded successor:
  making `setAttribute` resident in string `values` mode — which,
  because the key would then be device-produced, is also the change
  that would finally require the device-side counting sort this design
  avoids.
- three version dependency: three publishes no supported way to render
  from a buffer you already own, so the adapter seeds three's WebGPU
  backend attribute record (`renderer.backend.get(attribute).buffer`)
  to make three's own buffer creation and upload a no-op. Peer range
  `three@^0.185.1`, verified against `0.185.1`.
  `checkAdoptionSeam(renderer, makeAttribute)` (exported from
  `pcg-ts/three`) is the guard: it seeds a sentinel on a throwaway
  attribute, runs three's creation path over it, and verifies the
  sentinel survived. `createWebGpuInstanceAdapter` runs it at
  CONSTRUCTION — a moved internal fails at startup with an actionable
  message (pin three / update ADOPTION_SEAM / drop `deviceInstances`),
  never a silent fallback to wrong rendering.
- Determinism: the device compose is f32 throughout where CPU
  `composeTRS` keeps an f64 interior — a DOCUMENTED TOLERANCE CLASS,
  not a bit-exact port, because these bytes drive a renderer, not a
  seed chain. Measured over 4096 instances: translation column
  byte-identical always (straight copy of P); pad rows exact (3/7/11 =
  0, 15 = 1); absent rot/scale is BIT-EXACT end to end (compiled-in
  identity/one); basis deviation <= 1e-6 abs and <= 5e-8 of the basis
  range (measured 1.70e-8), >70% of the sample bit-equal; rot without
  scale measured max |cpu-gpu| = 1.19e-7. Run-to-run byte-identical on
  one device. Nothing else moves: determinism suites pin the CPU path,
  CPU goldens are unchanged, and no device-composed float feeds a seed,
  an index, or a later cook.

Determinism contract — the CPU is the bit-exact reference; existing
goldens never move:

- Bit-exact (byte equality): u32 hash/random streams (`randomField`
  with default and string keys, noise lattice hashing), `index`,
  u32/i32 attribute roots, bool→f32 reads, pure hash+compare+select
  trees, and f32 add/sub/mul, clamp/min/max, floor, select/compares.
- On one device, repeated dispatches are run-to-run byte-identical.
- Branchy ops (select, compares, ramp segments, worley cell walks) may
  flip at knife-edge inputs whose operands differ within tolerance.
- Everything else matches within measured budgets. Metric: rangeUlp =
  |cpu−gpu| / (2⁻²³ · max|cpu|) — ULPs at the top of the family's
  output range (raw max-ULP inflates at output zero-crossings, where
  the CPU's f64 interior survives cancellation that f32 cannot).
  Measured on discrete desktop hardware (D3D12/Dawn), 10 000 dense
  hash-derived inputs; budgets are the measured values rounded up
  minimally and may be exceeded on other adapters:

  | family | measured rangeUlp | budget |
  |---|---|---|
  | arith add/sub/mul | 0 | bit-exact |
  | clamp/min/max, floor, select/compare | 0 | bit-exact |
  | div | 0.76 | 1 |
  | lerp | 0.50 | 1 |
  | remap | 0.00 | 1 |
  | ramp (multi-stop) | 1.09 | 2 |
  | dot | 0.70 | 1 |
  | length/normalize (incl. sqrt) | 1.50 | 2 |
  | sin/cos over [−8, 8] | 6.50 | 8 |
  | tan over [−1.45, 1.45] | 19.48 | 24 |
  | asin over [−0.9, 0.9] | 503.99 | 512 |
  | acos over [−0.9, 0.9] | 359.09 | 384 |
  | atan | 67.06 | 80 |
  | atan2 | 64.52 | 80 |
  | valueNoise raw / normalized | 6.53 / 6.53 | 8 / 8 |
  | perlinNoise raw / normalized | 7.69 / 4.21 | 10 / 6 |
  | simplexNoise raw / normalized | 17.46 / 8.55 | 24 / 12 |
  | worley f1 / f2 | 5.16 / 4.71 | 8 / 8 |
  | worley f2−f1 normalized / exact f2−f1 | 9.42 / 9.28 | 12 / 12 |
  | fbm value / perlin / simplex / worley | 4.32 / 4.84 / 19.02 / 4.81 | 6 / 6 / 24 / 6 |
  | composite (ramp∘perlin × (random+attr)) | 9.77 | 12 |

  asin/acos absolute error ≈ 6.7e-5 — the WGSL-specified
  absolute-error class for those builtins.

- Per-node budgets for the field-driven point ops (same adapter,
  10k/8k points, perlin-normalized params):

  | node (noise-driven param) | measured | budget |
  |---|---|---|
  | transformPoints (translate) | rangeUlp 0.92 | 2 |
  | jitterPoints (amount) | rangeUlp 0.93 | 2 |
  | volumeSample (jitter) | rangeUlp 0.50 | 1 |
  | orientAlongVector (direction) | min quat dot 0.999999933 | ≥ 0.9999999 |
  | surfaceSample (density) | accept-set symDiff 0 / 4096 | ≤ 8 |

- Fused-run (composed) budgets, 17 device chains of 2–8 members:

  | chain | quantity | measured | budget |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | noise → orient → transform → jitter | P | rangeUlp 4.83 | ≤ 6 |
  | | perlin-normalized attr | rangeUlp 4.27 | ≤ 6 |
  | | rot | min quat dot 0.99999957 | ≥ 0.9999995 |
  | transform → orient → length | P / h | rangeUlp 1.69 / 1.71 | ≤ 3 |
  | orient → transform | P | rangeUlp 1.33 | ≤ 3 |

  12 of the 17 are BYTE-IDENTICAL to the CPU. That is engineered, not
  incidental: those chains use power-of-two jitter amounts and
  identity-euler / power-of-two transform scales, so every f32 step is
  exact and the single store is the only rounding. A non-pow2 jitter
  amount (`jitterPoints` rounds twice where the CPU rounds once) or a
  `quatFromBasis` rotation moves a chain into the budgeted class.

- All budgets above were measured on ONE adapter (discrete desktop,
  D3D12/Dawn) and are the measured values rounded up minimally. Another
  adapter exceeding one is a finding worth reporting, not expected
  noise.

Out-of-domain inputs are GIGO — measured and documented, not patched:

- min/max with a NaN operand: CPU propagates NaN; a GPU may return the
  non-NaN operand (any adapter must yield NaN or the other operand).
- |v| beyond f32 range: GPU length → Inf and normalize → 0 where the
  CPU's f64 interior survives (≈1.4e20); tiny |v| (≈1.4e-25)
  underflows both to 0 on GPU.
- Noise lattice coords ≥ 2³¹ diverge (JS ToUint32 wraps, WGSL f32→int
  saturates); ordinary lanes stay within the noise budget.
- Subnormal results flush to exactly 0 on GPU; CPU keeps subnormals.

## Errors

Read error messages: they name the offending node id, pin, or param and
list the valid alternatives (e.g. unknown node type errors list all
registered types; unknown field fn errors list all fns; pin errors list
valid pins). Typed classes: GraphValidationError, GraphCycleError,
NodeExecutionError (has .nodeId), CookCancelledError,
GraphSerializationError, FieldJsonError, WorldValidationError.

## Pointers

- README.md — human tour with runnable examples
- docs/nodes.md — full generated node reference (pins, params, defaults, ranges)
- docs/nodes.json — the same registry metadata, machine-readable
- docs/authoring.md — graph JSON spec, complete field grammar, recipes,
  GPU eligibility rules
- examples/ — nine vite demos; 06-graph-editor is an interactive node
  editor built on this same registry metadata and JSON format;
  08-gpu-fields cooks one five-node fusable chain three ways (CPU, GPU
  per-node, one fused device-resident run) with cold-cache wall times,
  the full CookStats.gpu counters, and a live parity readout;
  09-gpu-world streams a World rendering from device-resident instance
  transforms, with the binding's live handle count and the evaluator
  pool's detached-buffer accounting shown side by side; 02-forest is
  the MULTI-ASSET demonstration — `assetAttr: "species"` on the
  device-resident path, with a CPU/resident toggle, the per-asset batch
  count, and a fusion readout that does not overstate depth
